articles.body: MSC has opened a new headquarters in Abidjan, bringing its MSC, MEDLOG and TSP teams together in a single building. The new premises coincide with the container carrier’s 30th anniversary in Côte d’Ivoire and are intended to support its future development in the country. MSC operates from Abidjan and San Pedro, connecting Ivorian businesses and producers with regional and international markets. Côte d’Ivoire also forms part of the company’s wider West African network. Government and port representatives attend inauguration The opening ceremony was attended by customers, business partners and government representatives. Guests included Yacouba Sié, Côte d’Ivoire’s Minister of Infrastructure and Road Maintenance; representatives from the Swiss and Italian diplomatic missions; officials from the port authorities of Abidjan and San Pedro; and François Albert Amichia, Mayor of Treichville. “The inauguration of our new headquarters is an important milestone as we mark 30 years of MSC’s presence in Côte d’Ivoire,” said Cédric Goujon, Managing Director of MSC Côte d’Ivoire. “From Abidjan and San Pedro, our teams work closely with customers and partners to connect Ivorian businesses and producers with regional and international markets.” Goujon added that the new working environment reflects MSC’s confidence in Côte d’Ivoire and will support its continued development alongside local businesses and communities.

articles.title: Apache keeps North Sea assets producing despite worker walkouts
articles.summary: US energy company Apache said that production from its UK North Sea assets remains unaffected despite escalating industrial action involving around 170 offshore workers. Members of the Unite union staged a series of rolling strikes across seven Apache-operated installations over the weekend as part of an ongoing...
articles.body: Europe Offshore Apache keeps North Sea assets producing despite worker walkouts Bojan Lepic November 17, 2026 0 0 1 minute read Apache Apache US energy company Apache said that production from its UK North Sea assets remains unaffected despite escalating industrial action involving around 170 offshore workers. Members of the Unite union staged a series of rolling strikes across seven Apache-operated installations over the weekend as part of an ongoing dispute concerning pay and working conditions. Workers on Forties Alpha, Forties Bravo, Forties Delta, and Beryl Bravo walked out on November 13, followed by employees on Forties Charlie, Forties Echo, and Beryl Alpha on November 15. The latest action ended on Monday morning, with union members also staging a protest outside Apache’s Aberdeen headquarters. Unite claimed the action was disrupting offshore operations and accused the company of imposing below-inflation pay increases and maintaining an unfair seven-day clawback policy. Apache rejected the suggestion that production was affected, saying 49% of bargaining unit employees scheduled to work reported for duty during the strikes. The company said all its producing assets remained online and that neither the Forties Pipeline System nor the SAGE gas pipeline had been disrupted. Beryl Bravo was the only installation offline, although the platform is already undergoing decommissioning. Apache said its pay offer remained available and that it had invited UK conciliation service Acas to help resolve the dispute. The company previously offered workers a 4% pay increase, which Unite rejected. The strikes come as Apache prepares to end production from its UK North Sea assets by 2029, followed by the decommissioning of seven platforms and approximately 260 wells across the Forties and Beryl fields. articles.title: SFL expands Orca AI navigation technology across 44 vessels
articles.summary: SFL Corporation is expanding the deployment of Orca AI’s navigation technology across 44 vessels following an initial rollout that began in 2025. The agreement covers vessels across SFL’s shipping portfolio, as well as future newbuildings and vessels acquired through sale and purchase transactions. The expansion...
articles.body: SFL Corporation is expanding the deployment of Orca AI’s navigation technology across 44 vessels following an initial rollout that began in 2025. The agreement covers vessels across SFL’s shipping portfolio, as well as future newbuildings and vessels acquired through sale and purchase transactions. The expansion follows the deployment of Orca AI technology on five vessels in 2025. Over the following year, SFL tested the system during normal operations, with feedback from crews, technical managers and shore-based teams. The company now plans to extend the technology across a broader range of vessels to improve navigational safety and strengthen fleetwide risk monitoring. AI technology connects onboard and shore operations Orca AI uses artificial intelligence and computer vision to provide additional information to bridge teams. Its system offers 360-degree visual coverage around a vessel, including areas that may be difficult to monitor directly from the bridge. The technology also connects onboard navigational information with shore-based safety management. This allows shore teams to review navigational events and identify recurring risks across different vessels. The information can then support operational assessments and safety improvements throughout the fleet. However, the system does not replace the responsibility of the master or bridge team. Navigational decisions remain under their control. “Several situations over the past few years have shown us that bridge teams need better decision-making tools,” said Trym Otto Sjølie, Chief Operating Officer, SFL. “AI will have a significant impact on shipping, and its value will depend on how it is implemented. We are still in the early days, and SFL wants to take part in that development,” Sjølie added. The expanded deployment builds on SFL’s experience with the technology during the initial operational trials in Europe and Asia. Orca AI CEO and Co-founder Yarden Gross welcomed the agreement, highlighting SFL’s decision to introduce AI-assisted navigation on a larger scale. SFL’s fleet includes container vessels, car carriers, tankers, bulk carriers, gas carriers and offshore energy assets. Most of these vessels operate under long-term charter agreements. According to Orca AI, its platform is already used on more than 2,000 vessels worldwide. Its maritime customers include MSC, Seaspan, Eastern Pacific Shipping and NYK. The latest agreement adds SFL to the shipping companies expanding their use of AI-assisted navigation as part of fleet safety management.

articles.title: Shell kicks off gas production from its deepwater project in Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Shell has brought online a natural gas development off the coast of Malaysia, which is home to an offshore platform designed to run on solar energy.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 17, 2026 · 2 minutes ago Shell kicks off gas production from its deepwater project in Southeast Asia Shell has brought online a natural gas development off the coast of Malaysia, which is home to an offshore platform designed to run on solar energy. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Rosmari-Marjoram topside sailaway Source: Malaysia Marine and Heavy Engineering Holdings (MHB) Sarawak Shell, a subsidiary of the UK-headquartered energy giant Shell, has begun flowing the first gas from its deepwater fields off Sarawak, Malaysia, which are expected to support the company's production growth into the 2030s. Shell has started production from the Rosmari and Marjoram fields located 220 kilometers off the coast of Sarawak, bringing its latest development on stream four years after making a final investment decision (FID) in 2022 to develop the project, containing these deepwater sour gas fields discovered in 2014. " Shell is proud of its long and successful history in Malaysia. We have strong expertise in this basin, and the start-up of Rosmari-Marjoram contributes to production growth into the 2030s. This project builds on decades of experience to bring new gas supply online efficiently and competitively. " — Peter Costello President of Upstream The company explains that the gas produced from Rosmari-Marjoram will be piped to a new onshore gas plant in Bintulu, Sarawak, where it will be processed and fed to the Petronas LNG Complex . The development consists of a subsea tie-back, an unmanned wellhead platform, a 207-kilometer pipeline to shore, and an onshore gas plant at Bintulu. The project’s offshore platform is powered by solar panels , with back-up diesel generators available when needed. The onshore plant draws on the predominantly hydropower-based local electricity grid, supplemented by renewable energy certificates to achieve 100% renewable power. Related Articles Fossil Energy Shell’s new solar-powered platform with 20-year design life on its way to offshore gas field (Gallery) 2 min read " The offshore platform is designed to be powered by solar panels when it is unmanned, with batteries providing storage for up to three days of electricity. Diesel generators provide a backup source of electricity and help to power the platform when personnel visit for maintenance, which requires more energy to run ancillary services. The onshore gas plant is run on the equivalent of 100% hydropower, with renewable energy certificates complementing hydropower used directly from the electricity grid. " — Shell elaborated. The firm drilled Malaysia’s first oil well in 1910 and has been producing gas offshore since 1982. In addition to Rosmari-Marjoram, the company has interests in multiple producing fields off the coast of Sarawak, including Timi and Gorek , and is exploring other potential opportunities in the basin. According to Shell, Rosmari-Marjoram contributes to its commitment to deliver upstream and integrated gas projects coming on stream between 2025 and 2030 with a total peak production of more than 1.4 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (boe/d). Sarawak Shell is the operator of Rosmari-Marjoram, holding 71% equity, while its partners are Petronas Carigali, Inpex Malaysia E&P, and Searah. Reach the Offshore Energy industry in one go! articles.title: African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping
articles.summary: A growing group of African nations is pushing ahead with plans to introduce carbon charges on international shipping, raising the prospect of another regional emissions regime for shipowners already grappling with European environmental legislation. Guinea, Ivory Coast and Mauritania have signed an agreement at the...
articles.body: Africa Environment Regulatory African nations join forces to impose carbon charges on shipping Sam Chambers November 17, 2026 0 404 1 minute read Norden Norden A growing group of African nations is pushing ahead with plans to introduce carbon charges on international shipping, raising the prospect of another regional emissions regime for shipowners already grappling with European environmental legislation. Guinea, Ivory Coast and Mauritania have signed an agreement at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, to develop a coordinated approach to charging ships for their carbon emissions. The initiative, promoted by the Africa Sovereign Carbon Registry Foundation (ASCRF), builds on existing schemes in Djibouti and Gabon, with the ambition of establishing a continent-wide framework for raising climate finance from international shipping and aviation. Under the model pioneered by Djibouti, vessels are charged $17 per tonne of CO2 calculated on 50% of emissions from voyages to and from the country’s ports. Gabon has adopted a similar approach, increasing its own carbon charge in September. The revenues are intended to support national climate adaptation and energy transition projects. The latest agreement brings the number of countries associated with the proposed African coalition to six, although the status of Liberia’s involvement remains contentious. Monrovia stated earlier this year that it would not impose a unilateral carbon levy on international shipping. Other African countries are considering similar schemes. The development comes at a particularly sensitive moment for shipping’s decarbonisation negotiations, with the International Maritime Organization due to resume discussions on its proposed global emissions framework later this month. Unlike the EU Emissions Trading System, the African arrangements currently in force impose fixed charges rather than requiring companies to purchase tradable emissions allowances. No implementation dates or final charging arrangements have been announced for the three newest participating countries. articles.title: China emerges as dry bulk export powerhouse
articles.summary: China’s transformation from the world’s dominant dry bulk importer into an increasingly significant exporter is gathering pace, with outbound cargo volumes more than doubling since 2020 and accounting for nearly two-thirds of global dry bulk shipment growth this year. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers, using Signal...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Greater China China emerges as dry bulk export powerhouse Sam Chambers November 17, 2026 0 449 1 minute read China’s transformation from the world’s dominant dry bulk importer into an increasingly significant exporter is gathering pace, with outbound cargo volumes more than doubling since 2020 and accounting for nearly two-thirds of global dry bulk shipment growth this year. New analysis from Ursa Shipbrokers, using Signal Ocean vessel-tracking data, shows Chinese dry bulk loadings reached 274.9m tonnes in the first 10 months of 2026, up 14.9% year-on-year China accounted for 35.6m tonnes of the 54.4m-tonne increase in global dry bulk loadings during the period, an extraordinary contribution from a country traditionally viewed principally as a destination for raw materials. Its share of worldwide dry bulk loadings has climbed from just 2.5% in 2020 to 5.5% this year, with annual export shipments rising from 128.6m tonnes to 291.5m tonnes between 2020 and 2025. September set a new monthly record of 32.8m tonnes, while October’s 29.5m tonnes remained 12.8% above the corresponding month last year. The changing trade patterns are particularly significant for owners of handysize, supramax and ultramax vessels, which transport many of China’s outbound industrial commodities. The shift has not escaped the attention of leading dry bulk owners. “From being an almost sole importer of dry cargoes [China] has emerged into a large exporter over the last few years, a very interesting development indeed,” Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chairman and chief executive of Norwegian owner Belships, told Splash in an interview last week. China’s struggling property market has contributed to the change, with excess domestic production finding buyers overseas. Cement and clinker exports have climbed from negligible levels to around 25m tonnes in just a few years. Steel remains another major export commodity. Chinese customs figures show 95.5m tonnes of steel products were shipped overseas between January and October, although that represented a 2.3% decline from the corresponding period last year. BRS Shipbrokers recently reported an 18.5% increase in Chinese dry bulk export cargoes during the first nine months of 2026, reinforcing the broader trend identified by Ursa. The export boom is unfolding despite weakness in China’s domestic manufacturing economy, with October’s purchasing managers’ index slipping back into contraction territory. articles.title: ExxonMobil pushes ahead with Guyana’s eighth oil project as Saipem gets the all-clear and SBM Offshore bags FPSO job
articles.summary: Guyana’s deepwater expansion is gaining momentum as ExxonMobil moves to the execution phase of its recently sanctioned offshore oil development.
articles.body: Contracts & Tenders November 17, 2026 · 10 minutes ago ExxonMobil pushes ahead with Guyana’s eighth oil project as Saipem gets the all-clear and SBM Offshore bags FPSO job Guyana’s deepwater expansion is gaining momentum as ExxonMobil moves to the execution phase of its recently sanctioned offshore oil development. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Constellation Source: Saipem ExxonMobil Guyana, a subsidiary of the U.S.-headquartered energy giant ExxonMobil, has given Italy’s Saipem the go-ahead to proceed with the $1-1.5 billion subsea assignment on its eighth oil development project in the Stabroek block off the coast of Guyana and handed out a floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) award to the Netherlands-based SBM Offshore. Saipem has received the authorization to proceed with the execution of the Longtail project in Guyana’s Stabroek block, located at a water depth of approximately 1,750 meters. This comes shortly after ExxonMobil made a final investment decision (FID) for the eighth development on the offshore block and follows Saipem's announcement regarding the receipt of the limited notice to proceed (LNTP) in April 2026 to begin the preliminary activities for detailed engineering and procurement of long-lead equipment destined for the project. The contract, with an estimated overall value of between $1 billion and $1.5 billion, entails the engineering, procurement, construction, and installation (EPCI) of the subsea structures, umbilicals, risers, and flowlines (SURF) system. Following the receipt of the necessary government and regulatory approvals, as well as the FID for the project, the Italian giant is in the clear to continue with the execution of the remaining contract activities, with an expected duration of around four years. The company will perform offshore operations using vessels from its fleet, such as FDS2 , Castorone , and Constellation . Fabrication activities will be executed at Saipem's Italian yard in Arbatax, Sardinia, while logistics will be managed in Guyana through the Vreed-en-Hoop Shorebase Inc. (VEHSI) yard, involving the local supply chain and resources. “With the Longtail project, Saipem confirms its presence in a strategic country, where it has already been awarded seven offshore development contracts by ExxonMobil Guyana Limited, namely Liza Phase 1 and Phase 2, Payara, Yellowtail, Uaru, Whiptail and Hammerhead,” emphasized the Italian company. Related Articles Project & Tenders ExxonMobil reaches FID on eighth project offshore Guyana 2 min read Meanwhile, SBM Offshore has been awarded contracts by ExxonMobil Guyana for the same development project to construct and install an FPSO, which it expects to operate for an initial period of ten years, combining the strengths of both companies and leveraging the expertise, experience, and operational excellence of the FPSOs currently deployed in the Stabroek block. The award follows completion of front-end engineering and design (FEED) studies and the final investment decision on the project by the operator and its block co-venturers. The FPSO design is based on SBM Offshore’s Fast4Ward program, incorporating the company’s tenth new-build multi-purpose floater hull. The FPSO, which will be designed to produce and process 1.2 billion standard cubic feet of gas per day and 250,000 barrels of condensate per day, will be spread moored in a water depth of about 1,750 meters and able to store around 2 million barrels of condensate. " We are proud to receive this sixth FPSO award from ExxonMobil Guyana. This milestone demonstrates our strong collaboration with ExxonMobil and highlights the strength of our Fast4Ward program, which industrializes complex deepwater developments through standardized design, disciplined execution and the transfer of lifecycle learnings across our fleet. Combined with a culture of continuous improvement and a relentless pursuit of excellence, this approach allows us to continuously evolve our solutions, accelerate delivery and create lasting value for our clients. " — Øivind Tangen Chief Executive Officer of SBM Offshore Building on the experience gained from the FPSOs Liza Destiny , Liza Unity , Prosperity , One Guyana , and Jaguar , SBM Offshore emphasizes that it remains committed to supporting local content development in Guyana by expanding its collaboration with Guyanese companies, sourcing fabrication scope locally, and recruiting and integrating Guyanese engineers into both the execution and operational teams, including the FPSO project team. ExxonMobil Guyana operates the Stabroek block and has a 45% interest, with Hess Guyana Exploration, part of Chevron, owning 30%, and CNOOC Petroleum Guyana holding the remaining 25%. The latest set of awards follows on the heels of ExxonMobil’s start-up of Uaru , its fifth development in the Stabroek block, lifting the country’s installed production capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day. Leveraging our extensive expertise in large-scale gas-processing systems and our proven track record in Guyana, SBM Offshore is well positioned to support the Longtail development, which will require the highest gas-handling capacity ever deployed on an FPSO, while delivering safe, reliable and efficient operations. articles.title: Hong Kong’s shipowner dynasties face the succession test
articles.summary: The city’s great shipping families have survived every imaginable market shock. Keeping the next generation – and its capital – anchored in Hong Kong may prove a different challenge. The latest chapter from our brand new Hong Kong magazine, which is being distributed across the city’s maritime week. Three sets of...
articles.body: Greater China Hong Kong’s shipowner dynasties face the succession test Splash November 17, 2026 0 1,981 4 minutes read Zhejiang University Zhejiang University The city’s great shipping families have survived every imaginable market shock. Keeping the next generation – and its capital – anchored in Hong Kong may prove a different challenge. The latest chapter from our brand new Hong Kong magazine, which is being distributed across the city’s maritime week. Three sets of initials still define Hong Kong’s rise as a shipowning powerhouse: Y.K. Pao (pictured), C.Y. Tung and T.Y. Chao. Their generation transformed a trading entrepôt into one of the world’s great centres of private shipownership, building fleets across oceans and relationships across political divides. What they created was more than a collection of ships. It was a distinctive business culture: discreet, entrepreneurial, internationally connected and, despite the huge sums involved, keenly aware of financial risk and the danger of assuming that a freight boom will last forever. Its strength has always been an ability to think in decades while trading in markets that can turn in weeks. That instinct is hard earned, not evidence of perfect judgement. The debt crisis that engulfed Orient Overseas following C.Y. Tung’s death in 1982 is a reminder that even the city’s most celebrated shipowners have misread a cycle. Hong Kong’s commercial memory includes the failures as well as the fortunes. Now the question is whether those instincts can survive another transition: the transfer of control to generations with more ways than ever to invest their inheritance, and more places from which to run a shipping business. Richard Hext, chairman of the Hong Kong Shipowners Association (HKSOA), describes owners who combine “global ambition with a healthy respect for cycles”. They have lived through recessions, SARS, the pandemic and repeated geopolitical shocks, he says, and learned to protect liquidity, limit leverage and stay close to their customers and ships. It is a substantial community. HKSOA members owned, managed or operated around 180m dwt at the end of 2025. Those figures are not a count of vessels directly owned by Hong Kong families, but they demonstrate the continuing heft of the wider owner-manager network. Hext also points to owners’ involvement in safety, decarbonisation and talent development. “Those are not the behaviours of a community that has lost interest in its industry,” he says. Nor has this decade been uniformly miserable for owners. Pandemic-era disruption brought extraordinary returns in some segments, while subsequent wars, rerouting, sanctions and trade tensions created both windfalls and frightening exposure. The successful Hong Kong response has generally been less about calling every market turn than ensuring a business can withstand the next one. Niraj Nanda, chief commercial officer at Anglo-Eastern, points to selective fleet renewal, disposals at attractive prices and the retention of cash. “In a cyclical business, the important discipline is to use the good years not only to grow, but also to prepare for the rainy day that will eventually come,” he says. That conservatism should not be confused with timidity. Wah Kwong Maritime Transport, founded by T.Y. Chao in 1952 and now led by the family’s third generation, has launched Wah Kwong Bulk with ambitions to operate 50 to 60 vessels by 2030. It has also ordered new LR2 tankers and moved into port electrification through its Wah Kwong NatPower venture. This is a traditional shipowning name extending its reach rather than retreating. Elsewhere, Valles Steamship remains in the hands of the Koo family, with a fourth generation involved in the business. The Tung family provides a more complicated illustration of continuity. It sold its flagship liner business, OOCL, to COSCO in 2018, but continues to operate in shipping through the much smaller, privately held Island Navigation. The scale changes; the maritime inheritance survives. The Banga family offers another contemporary succession story. Angad Banga succeeded his father Harry as chief executive of The Caravel Group this year, taking responsibility for a business spanning ships, shipmanagement, commodities and investments, including a significant shareholding in Pacific Basin. “For our family, shipping is not simply an asset class. It is an industry we believe in deeply,” Banga says. His emphasis is on stewardship rather than reinventing the business, and on leaving it stronger for those who follow. Firoze Mirza, chairman of BSM Hong Kong, observes that several established families now have “third and fourth generations in the saddle”. But the picture is not universal. Some heirs regard shipping as a vocation; others see one investment among many. Bjorn Hojgaard, chief executive of Anglo-Eastern, is candid about the change. “The picture is mixed, and it would be unfair to generalise,” he says. Families increasingly manage wealth through professional structures, allocating money across property, private credit, technology and other investments. For some, shipping becomes one component of a diversified portfolio rather than the organising purpose of the family business. Vikrant Gusain, chief executive of Dockendale Group, puts the succession challenge sharply: “Shipping therefore has to compete for family capital rather than assume it will inherit it.” More importantly, he argues, the next generation must be able to build a modern shipping enterprise in Hong Kong, not simply administer ships acquired by their parents or grandparents. That brings the debate beyond family loyalty to the city’s competitiveness. Gautam Chellaram, chairman of KC Maritime, identifies “domicile drift” as a particular danger: internationally educated, mobile heirs can put family offices, investment mandates and commercial decisions wherever regulation, costs and opportunities suit them best. Recent events show how quickly that can happen. Hong Kong-listed Pacific Basin moved strategic leadership and commercial decision-making to Singapore in 2025 amid US-China port-fee tensions, while Seaspan also relocated its headquarters to the city-state. The subsequent suspension of those fees does not undo the lesson: the location of a vessel’s flag, its ownership company and the people making decisions can change with remarkable speed. The threat, therefore, is not an imminent extinction of Hong Kong’s shipping families. It is a gradual thinning out of the city’s decision-making ecosystem. If the next generation continues to own vessels but chooses to finance, charter and direct them elsewhere, Hong Kong can retain impressive maritime statistics while losing some of the commercial influence that made those statistics possible. Survival, though, is not quite the same as renewal. Hong Kong needs new principals willing to build companies, not only heirs prepared to preserve existing ones. The survival of this unique breed ultimately depends on more than inherited loyalty. The city must remain somewhere a young owner wants to take risk, build relationships, hire talent and commit capital. articles.body: Europe Operations Fresh strike threat hangs over ITF leadership Adis Ajdin November 17, 2026 0 95 1 minute read ITF Accountability ITF Accountability Workers at the International Transport Workers’ Federation (ITF) have voted for fresh strike action, putting the global union organisation on a collision course with its own staff once again over pay, working conditions and collective bargaining rights. A postal ballot of Unite members at the ITF’s London headquarters saw 74% back industrial action on an 83% turnout. The vote marks the third strike mandate secured by ITF staff since July last year, when a bitter dispute erupted over plans to slash the organisation’s workforce. The latest confrontation centres on management’s proposed changes to the staff collective bargaining agreement, with union representatives claiming the ITF has threatened to impose new employment terms if a replacement deal is not reached by January 1, 2027. Workers have also challenged the handling of grievances involving two dismissed union representatives and raised continuing concerns over workplace equality. The ITF Staff Union, which represents employees through Unite, said members would not accept the abandonment of their collective agreement or what it described as inferior employment conditions. According to ITF Accountability, a campaign backed by current and former staff and affiliated union members, the Unite bargaining unit has shrunk by 37% since July 2025 following a major restructuring programme. The dispute dates back to last year, when ITF management unveiled plans to cut around a quarter of its London workforce. More than 100 employees subsequently staged a four-day walkout in September 2025, the first strike in the federation’s nearly 130-year history. Tensions escalated further in January this year when two union representatives were dismissed, prompting Unite to challenge the decisions and accuse management of targeting union activists. The latest standoff comes with the ITF still facing scrutiny over allegations of harassment, sexism and discrimination within its leadership and workplace culture. The federation’s executive board commissioned an independent investigation into those allegations, overseen by its Affiliate Oversight Group, with submissions closing at the end of September. Further negotiations between management and staff representatives are scheduled between November 19 and December 15.No dates have yet been announced for a fresh walkout. articles.title: The East India company without a charter
articles.summary: Carriers and port groups are rebuilding the oldest form of trade finance – financing the cargo they carry. Sergey Belskiy from Metal Supply Experts follows the money from Venice to DP World and asks who pays. In July 2025, DP World reported that its finance arm had financed more than $1 billion of trade. articles.body: Contributions Finance and Insurance Operations The East India company without a charter Splash November 17, 2026 0 523 6 minutes read Carriers and port groups are rebuilding the oldest form of trade finance – financing the cargo they carry. Sergey Belskiy from Metal Supply Experts follows the money from Venice to DP World and asks who pays. In July 2025, DP World reported that its finance arm had financed more than $1 billion of trade. Behind it stand 32 financial institutions, among them J.P. Morgan, which has shared risk with a port operator since June 2025. By December, the Asian Development Bank was still putting the trade finance gap at $2.5 trillion, with 41% of applications from small and medium-sized enterprises refused. The bank that turns a client away at its own counter is financing him through the owner of the terminal. Trade finance is passing from banks to the owners of the cargo flow – shipping lines, port and logistics groups, and their trading subsidiaries. Not because the banks have run out of money. And the cargo owner will pay for the move in something other than interest. What the bank is short of Capital has not left trade finance: at the top it is in surplus, and the shortage is of bankable structure. Two things decide what follows. Holding a short trade asset on a bank balance sheet has become expensive, so the money is accumulating elsewhere. And checking a mid-market file costs a bank more than the fee earns, because knowledge of the goods sits with whoever sails the ship, runs the terminal and issues the bill of lading, for whom the counterparty check is a by-product of the booking. Hence the rule that governs this market’s whole history: trade is financed by whoever holds the mobile capital of the day, and knowledge of the goods decides only through whose hands that capital reaches the cargo. Goods, carriage and money have twice come together in one pair of hands and twice come apart. DP World is the third time, and the order of that alternation says how large it will be – and who will pay. The spiral Venice from the eleventh to the fourteenth century financed trade voyage by voyage. Money was not scarce, but there was no instrument to keep it: the sea loan and later the colleganza gathered it into a single voyage – a doge held half his fortune in such contracts – and dissolved on the ship’s return. One contract, one voyage – that was the ceiling. What changed in Genoa was the form of the claim. The commune, at war almost without pause, borrowed from its own citizens and cut the debt into shares that transferred by a simple ledger entry. For the first time capital could be held and passed on without entering any venture. Trade finance went to the class that lived on those claims – the banking house, lending at interest. From that day the merchant, risking nothing himself, pays those who go to sea. Genoa had fortresses, a transferable share and durable institutions – the Maona of Chios lasted until 1566 – but not broad accumulation: its shareholders were the commune’s own creditors, the same closed circle. The East India companies became possible where accumulation broke out of that circle. The 1602 subscription of the Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC) raised about 6.4 million guilders, and in the Amsterdam chamber alone 1,143 people subscribed, a maidservant among them. Only one form gathers a mass like that: joint-stock capital locked in for ten years – in practice never returned – with a share the investor could not redeem, only sell on. The VOC produced the exchange, not the reverse. Its charter gave it a monopoly too, and the shipper got one buyer where he had had a market. The nineteenth century pulled everything apart again, and again capital decided it. The industrial revolution gathered the short-term part of its surplus into the deposits of joint-stock banks. The London deposit bank lent thousands of other people’s balances, so trade was financed by the custodian of capital rather than its owner, at a price no private fortune could match. By 1913 roughly half of world trade ran on sterling bills drawn on London. Steam, the Suez Canal and the telegraph merely let that capital reach goods it never saw. Every time financing left the cargo flow, it built an instrument that had not existed before: Genoa made the claim transferable, the nineteenth century built the deposit bank, the money market and negotiable title. Every time it returned, it returned holding that instrument, and so at a larger scale. Venice joined goods, carriage and money within a voyage. The East India companies joined them within a firm that outlived its founders, on the Genoese share, and this time they are being joined across a network, on everything the banks built: their money market funds it, their negotiable title has gone electronic. Two conclusions follow. First, the cargo owner won exactly once – when the function went to a bank that owned neither ship nor goods, and money was cheaper than ever. He lost every time financing passed to someone who also had the disposal of his cargo. Second, this convergence will exceed the last one by as much as the banking instrument exceeds the Genoese share. Why now Capital has moved again. Money looking for yield is going past the banks, and the carriers have capital of their own: the container lines’ combined net profit over 2021 and 2022 came to some $364 billion, after twelve years in which the industry’s cumulative bottom line was negative. Knowledge of the goods, a public good for a century and a half, has become private again – it now sits inside the carrier’s system – and title is following. Since September 2023 the UK Electronic Trade Documents Act has given the electronic bill of lading the force of paper, and the FIT Alliance’s October survey puts adoption at 51.1%, with only 22.2% of banks reporting any use at all. The same order explains the earlier failures. Maersk piloted lending to shippers in India in 2016, and the product stayed niche for close to a decade: nothing scalable can be built on a paper bill of lading that travels by courier. TradeLens, the neutral platform Maersk built with IBM, closed in 2023 for want of the industry-wide collaboration it depended on. A platform has no cargo flow of its own. The exception is the Japanese sogo shosha, which never separated trading, carriage and finance. Berkshire Hathaway began buying into all five of them in 2019 and by September 2026 held more than 10% of each, a ceiling it had promised never to cross and the houses agreed to lift, with a stated horizon of fifty years or forever. The most conservative capital in the world saw the form before the market had a name for it. The form is a buy-back, not a loan Credit is transitional. The flow owner’s logic leads to a buy-back. The group’s trading subsidiary buys the goods from the client, carries them on the group’s ships under its own electronic bill of lading, and sells them back to the client, or to a buyer the client names, at the discharge port, on deferred terms and at a price that includes the cost of money. In law it is a sale. In economics it is financing secured on the goods themselves, with title held by the financing party throughout. The agreed repurchase closes the price risk, and where it fails the cargo goes to another buyer in the group’s network. The borrower’s credit risk becomes resale risk, which is what a global carrier carries better than a bank: a bank can take title too, but it cannot sell the cargo on. A company that buys and sells goods is not a bank, and bank capital requirements do not reach it. What is left for the banks is the wholesale money – the J.P. Morgan arrangement with DP World is the prototype. Are we heading for new East India companies? Yes, but not the ones people expect. No charters, no garrisons, no flag: what is being rebuilt is the commercial core – one counterparty owning the ship, the terminal, title to the cargo and the money advanced against it. The monopoly comes not from an exclusive right but from the bundle: every line in it is competitive on its own – freight, storage, finance – but they are quoted as one number. The structure has three limits, and two work by themselves: the groups compete, and supervision is already looking this way – the US Federal Maritime Commission counted some $15.4 billion of demurrage and detention collected by nine carriers over five years. The third has to be built into the transaction: someone on the cargo owner’s side alone, who takes the bundle apart and puts an alternative against each line of that one number. An honest boundary: the flow owner will finance what he carries and can see, and that will not close $2.5 trillion. Capital is waiting for a structure it can buy. It is now clear who will present it and what it stands on: the instrument the banks spent a century and a half building. What remains open is whether the cargo owner walks into it with an alternative in hand. For a century and a half he could afford not to think about that: the money came from someone with no use for his cargo. That period is ending. REUTERS/Stringer Two tankers were reportedly attacked in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, November 16, with both incidents resulting in engine-room fires and one vessel left disabled, according to separate warnings issued by United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO). The latest incident occurred at approximately 1900 UTC, about seven nautical miles north of Khasab, Oman. According to UKMTO, a third party reported that a tanker transiting the strategic waterway had been attacked, leaving the vessel disabled and causing a fire in its engine room. The crew was reported safe, although the extent of damage and any environmental impact remained unknown. Earlier Monday, at approximately 0558 UTC, the company security officer of another tanker reported that the vessel had been struck by an unidentified projectile while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz. The impact sparked a fire in the engine room, according to UKMTO. No casualties were reported, and all crew members were accounted for. The vessel’s condition and any potential environmental damage remained under assessment. The incidents follow another reported tanker attack on Sunday, November 15, when Indian shipping authorities notified UKMTO that a vessel had been attacked while traveling eastbound through the Arabian Gulf toward the Strait of Hormuz. All crew members were reported safe. The latest attacks come amid a sustained campaign of violence against commercial shipping in and around the waterway. JMIC reported five attacks off Oman’s Musandam Peninsula since November 1 and said maritime traffic remained substantially below prewar levels. The center also reported approximately 227 commercial vessels stationary at major anchorages east of the Strait of Hormuz, including Fujairah, Khor Fakkan, Sohar and Musandam, as restricted transit continues to create a persistent backlog. The latest JMIC assessment recorded 83 U.S.-facilitated transits between November 12 and 14, while separately tracked, non-facilitated commercial traffic remained at single-digit to low-double-digit levels per day. Those figures cover different vessel populations and should not be treated as directly comparable. UKMTO has not identified the vessels involved in Monday’s reported attacks or attributed responsibility. Authorities are investigating both incidents, and vessels operating in the region have been advised to exercise caution and report suspicious activity. REUTERS/Thomas Peter A Somali-flagged cargo ship carrying nearly 3,000 metric tons of wheat capsized off Bulgaria on Monday after what crew members described as an attack by two sea drones, marking the latest in a growing series of strikes against commercial shipping in the Black Sea. All 12 crew members aboard the BETUL 8 were rescued in an operation involving Bulgarian military helicopters and naval vessels from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey. According to Bulgaria’s Ministry of Transport and Communications , the Maritime Rescue Coordination Center in Varna received a distress call at approximately 9:15 a.m. local time reporting that the vessel was sinking about 40 nautical miles southeast of Cape Kaliakra, within Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. The vessel was sailing from Tulcea, Romania, to Egypt with a cargo of bulk wheat. Bulgarian maritime news outlet Maritime.bg , which spoke with surviving crew members, reported that two unmanned surface vessels struck the ship before it capsized. The publication also obtained photographs from the crew purportedly showing the drones involved in the attack. Survivors separately described the attack to Bulgarian National Television . Bulgarian authorities have not publicly identified who was responsible for the reported attack, and the origin of the drones remains unconfirmed. The rescue operation involved four vessels from the multinational Black Sea Mine Countermeasures Group, along with two Bulgarian Air Force Cougar helicopters and an Su-25 aircraft deployed to survey the area. The helicopters reached the scene and evacuated the crew from life rafts using rescue baskets. All 12 seafarers were transported to Bulgaria’s Chaika Naval Helicopter Air Base. The Bulgarian Transport Ministry said the survivors were in generally good condition, although they were suffering from exposure to the cold. Bulgarian naval officials later reported that one crew member had sustained a minor cut to the head. An aerial survey confirmed that the vessel had overturned. Bulgarian naval officials said the ship was lying upside down, with part of its bow remaining above the water. A naval vessel was dispatched to assess potential marine pollution. There was no immediate confirmation of an oil spill or other environmental damage. The incident comes amid an escalating series of attacks on merchant vessels operating near the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, raising concerns about the safety of commercial shipping routes in the western Black Sea. On Sunday, gCaptain reported that three commercial vessels had been struck by drones near Romania’s Sulina canal , a critical shipping corridor connecting the Danube River with the Black Sea. Romanian authorities reported no casualties in those attacks. The latest incident underscores the growing risks to merchant ships operating in waters bordering NATO members Romania and Bulgaria as the maritime consequences of the Russia-Ukraine war continue to spread. The cause of the BETUL 8 casualty and responsibility for the reported drone attack remain under investigation. articles.body: Singapore-based technology company Univers has announced a partnership with the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping to explore the role of artificial intelligence in maritime operations and decarbonisation. The agreement was formalised at the Singapore Pavilion during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, as part of a series of partnerships announced by Univers on 16 November 2026. The collaboration will examine how AI can support operational decisions across vessels, fuels, ports and other parts of the maritime supply chain. It will also explore how improved decision-making could deliver economic and environmental benefits. Univers will become one of the Center’s early AI partners, contributing its experience in connecting operational systems, data and artificial intelligence. New framework examines the value of AI in shipping A central part of the collaboration is Univers’ new Return on Intelligence framework. The approach aims to assess the business value generated by AI-driven decisions in physical operations. Rather than focusing only on technical performance or emissions reductions, the framework considers wider operational and financial outcomes. These include improved asset productivity, operating efficiency and potential opportunities for business growth. Univers has also introduced a whitepaper titled Return on Intelligence: How AI Changes the Economics of Transport , developed with input from the Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping. The document explores how organisations can evaluate the economic and environmental value of using AI in transport operations. “Maritime decarbonisation is a systems challenge. AI has the potential to connect decisions across vessels, fuels, ports and operations, translating intelligence into measurable operational, economic and environmental outcomes,” said Pernille Dahlgaard, Chief Impact Officer, Mærsk Mc-Kinney Møller Center for Zero Carbon Shipping. Univers’ Physical AI platform combines operational technology, information systems and AI to support the management of complex infrastructure. The company believes this approach could help maritime organisations improve coordination and make better use of operational information. However, the partners have not announced a specific vessel deployment, commercial implementation or timetable for introducing the technology into shipping operations. The maritime collaboration forms part of Univers’ wider expansion of AI applications across transport, energy and infrastructure. At COP31, the company also announced separate partnerships with the World Green Building Council and XIBER Energy Solutions.

BAE Systems, acting as the prime supplier, selected LALIZAS UK and Star International to provide lifesaving equipment for different Royal Navy applications. The contract covers commercially available LALIZAS lifejackets for training and water-activity centres, alongside bespoke equipment designed for personnel serving aboard Royal Navy vessels. Equipment undergoes extensive testing The selected lifejackets underwent trials assessing their suitability across a range of operational environments. According to the companies, the evaluation programme examined the durability and reliability of the equipment under demanding conditions. Specialists from LALIZAS UK and Star International also worked with Royal Navy personnel, providing product familiarisation and training to support the use of the selected equipment. “The programme has demonstrated the quality and reliability of the selected LALIZAS lifejacket solutions, supported by close collaboration between all parties involved,” said Philip Kleinot, Country Manager at LALIZAS UK. “We are pleased to be working with Star International to support the Royal Navy with equipment selected for its operational requirements.” Matt Ball, Managing Director at Star International, said the award reflected the cooperation between the two companies and the work undertaken during the evaluation process. “Supplying lifesaving equipment into demanding maritime environments requires close attention to product suitability, reliability and practical support, and we are proud to have played our part in this programme,” he added.

articles.title: The Oil Market Is Brimming With Crude Despite Tanker Attacks
articles.summary: More than eight months into the Iran war, smoke continues to billow from oil tankers as Tehran presses ahead with repeated attacks near the Strait of Hormuz.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. REUTERS/Ints Kalnins By Alex Longley, Anthony Di Paola, Shariq Khan and Mia Gindis (Bloomberg) — More than eight months into the Iran war, smoke continues to billow from oil tankers as Tehran presses ahead with repeated attacks near the Strait of Hormuz . And yet there’s more than enough crude on the global market. Saudi Arabia, the de facto leader of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries, said it pumped 10.5 million barrels a day in October, a level reached only once since 2022. Iraq and Kuwait also reported big increases, while the United Arab Emirates is now free of OPEC quotas, allowing it to pump as much as it wants. Gulf shipments nudged lower this week, but remain healthy despite a slew of attacks, according to TankerTrackers.com Inc. The ample supply has added to pressure on oil prices. Futures at one point this week were down almost 25% for the month, easing inflation concerns and offering respite for the global economy. Prices for physical cargoes have also plummeted, as producers compete for customers and exorbitant shipping costs begin to thaw. The recovery is still precarious. Attacks have killed at least one seafarer this month and spilled oil is washing ashore on the region’s beaches. With shipping under constant threat and Iranian media claiming attacks on navigational equipment near Hormuz, oil flows are erratic and could slow at any moment. But Emirati officials at a recent conference in Abu Dhabi were keen to stress the resilience of the industry. That ability to keep crude flowing, mirrored across the Gulf, has helped bring Middle East shipments back toward pre-war levels and pushed Brent crude prices below $90 a barrel at one point this week. “For us national shipping companies, there is no choice,” Khalid Alhammad, president of ship management for Saudi vessel owner Bahri, said at a conference in Dubai. “We still have to go through the Strait of Hormuz. We have to keep moving the energy.” It’s a remarkable turnaround from some of the worst fears at the outset of the war. Before the conflict, about a fifth of the world’s oil flowed through Hormuz, and analysts warned that a closure could send crude prices above $200 a barrel. Last week at Adipec, the Middle East’s biggest oil conference, senior executives agreed that crude markets look well supplied heading into 2027, with further price declines potentially easing the fight against inflation, though efforts to rebuild stockpiles depleted during the war could limit how far they fall. The recovery reached a milestone Friday, when the International Energy Agency said oil supply was outpacing demand for the first time since the war began. Rising production beyond the Gulf has helped cushion global markets, with weekly US crude output topping 14 million barrels a day for the first time and the latest figures from Brazil and Guyana all at records. The IEA said the shift, alongside a plunge in physical crude prices, suggested the market was “showing tentative signs of rebalancing.” Pockets of tightness persist. Fuel prices remain far higher than crude, with European diesel trading at about $170 a barrel, for example. Shipping costs are also still historically elevated. Transporting crude from the US to Asia adds roughly 20% to the price of American oil, more than double the premium a year ago. Yet even those strains have eased. Freight markets remain elevated, but are well below the extremes seen a month ago. US retail gasoline prices have also fallen below $4 a gallon for the first time since July, according to the American Automobile Association. “The return of supply from the Gulf has depressed prices, coupled with the deflation of the freight bubble,” said Sasha Foss, an analyst at Marex Group’s CSC Commodities. “The market is less stressed than it was, but October was the biggest month for vessel incidents in Hormuz, so there are still risks.” The rebalancing has come at a cost. Vitol Group, the world’s top independent oil trader, said recently that the Iran war has cut global oil consumption by about 3 million barrels a day, an assessment echoed by other major traders. The market, in other words, is finding its footing partly because the war has sharply curtailed demand across fuels and regions. China’s crude imports fell about 15% from a year earlier to 9.9 million barrels a day in October. European nations have reported double-digit declines in diesel demand, while US gasoline consumption was marginally lower than a year earlier during the peak summer driving season. The supply recovery began in earnest over the summer and has gathered pace since then. It shows up in a steady uptick in ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman, as traders unload cargoes onto new ships just outside Hormuz as part of a burgeoning shuttle trade. It has left traders with plenty of cargoes to sell. This week, Abu Dhabi National Oil Co. slashed the price of its flagship crude grade to attract buyers. Saudi Arabia also cut its key oil prices, though the kingdom is selling fewer barrels under long-term contracts than before the war, making its pricing harder to track. Instead, it has increasingly turned to ad hoc sales. The cuts underscore just how much oil is leaving the Gulf, even as tankers remain under attack. “The workarounds and the shuttle system have managed to keep these prices from going sky-high,” said John Kilduff, partner at Again Capital. “There’s a question of durability. We’ve gone through a period where the Iranians didn’t cause much havoc in the Strait. But lately, that’s ramped up again, and there’s a concern that this could go off the rails.” © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Avigator Fortuner/Shutterstock The gradual return of container shipping services to the Suez Canal is expected to release vessel capacity absorbed by lengthy diversions around Africa, but persistent port congestion and major network adjustments could keep supply chains under pressure well into 2027, according to DHL Global Forwarding. In a market assessment published Monday , DHL said more than 10% of the global container shipping fleet remains tied up in port congestion, representing approximately 3.6 million TEU of capacity. The bottlenecks persist even as carriers begin restoring services through the Red Sea and Suez Canal. Around 60% of relevant Asia-Europe headhaul services are currently planned to operate through Suez, although the return remains uneven across trade lanes, DHL said. The transition could take another six to 12 months as carriers reposition vessels, rebalance schedules and adjust networks that have spent years operating around the Cape of Good Hope. That timeline assumes security conditions do not force further changes. The assessment comes as Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd announced additional structural changes to their Gemini Cooperation services through the Suez Canal, marking another step toward restoring traditional Asia-Europe shipping routes. While shorter voyages free up vessels previously committed to longer routes, DHL warned that the additional capacity will not necessarily translate into reliable schedules. “Carriers must reposition ships, rebalance schedules and manage services operating across different routings,” said Bjoern Schoon, Senior Vice President of Ocean Freight at DHL Global Forwarding Asia Pacific. The changes are unfolding as the global containership fleet continues to expand. DHL’s November Ocean Freight Market Update forecasts fleet capacity growth of approximately 4% in 2026, while global ocean freight demand has increased 5% year to date. Meanwhile, DHL cited Linerlytica data showing that containership orders reached 6.4 million TEU so far this year, bringing the orderbook to approximately 47.8% of the active fleet. The combination of new ships, shorter Suez voyages and ongoing port congestion is creating increasingly uneven market conditions. DHL said freight rates are showing signs of weakness on some Asia-Europe services, while the transpacific market remains comparatively firm. In the Middle East, strong demand and severe congestion continue to support higher rates, with berth delays exceeding two weeks at some Gulf gateways. For shippers, the result is a market where additional fleet capacity does not necessarily mean faster or more dependable cargo movements. The logistics company expects schedule reliability, rather than available capacity alone, to remain a key challenge as shipping networks adjust through 2027. articles.title: The Future of Maritime Safety: Navigating the Polar Frontier’s Uncharted Waters and Hidden Hazards
articles.summary: The Arctic and Antarctic are increasingly becoming areas of convergence for maritime industries and government operations. Commercial shipping, offshore energy, expedition cruising, recreational yachting, scientific research, coast guard, and naval...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network The Arctic and Antarctic are increasingly becoming areas of convergence for maritime industries and government operations. Commercial shipping, offshore energy, expedition cruising, recreational yachting, scientific research, coast guard, and naval operations are all placing greater attention on these remote regions. For some, polar waters offer access to untapped natural resources and emerging shipping routes. For others, they provide opportunities for exploration, scientific discovery, and strategic operations in areas of growing geopolitical importance. But operating in these environments presents a unique set of challenges. Extreme weather, floating ice, limited infrastructure, and vast distances from support resources compound the risks associated with maritime operations. Even routine navigational decisions can carry significantly greater consequences when rescue capabilities and emergency response resources are hours or days away. Furthermore, the environmental sensitivity of these regions means that groundings, collisions, and pollution incidents can have lasting consequences. Understanding the environment above and below the waterline is critical to navigating these unforgiving waters. While radar, electronic charts, and other conventional navigation systems remain essential tools, they cannot always provide a complete picture of the hazards that lie ahead. In regions where chart data is sparse, satellite positioning can be degraded, and submerged hazards remain hidden from view, real-time underwater perception becomes an important part of safe vessel operations. For 25 years, FarSounder has developed technology to help mariners better understand their surroundings and navigate with greater confidence. Today, FarSounder’s Argos 3D Forward Looking Sonars are deployed on vessels operating in polar environments, including expedition cruise ships, polar research vessels, and naval platforms, some of which are icebreakers. These vessels leverage real-time awareness of the underwater environment to safely navigate some of the most remote and challenging waters on Earth. Navigating in Polar Regions Polar operations introduce unique hazards that complicate even the most routine maritime activities. Floating ice presents a significant navigational risk, as the visible portion above the surface may not accurately represent the size and shape of submerged ice keels below the waterline. Icebergs and other large ice masses can extend considerable distances beneath the surface, creating hazards that are difficult to assess through visual observation alone. The seafloor presents another challenge. In these regions, accurate chart data is sparse or nonexistent, leaving shallow bottoms, rocky pinnacles, and other underwater obstructions hidden. Even where charts are available, the underlying survey data may be outdated or lack the resolution necessary for safe navigation in unfamiliar waters. Navigation is further complicated by harsh weather conditions. High-latitude environments and magnetic anomalies can degrade the reliability of GPS and other positioning systems. Satellite communications may be intermittent, limiting a vessel’s ability to access external information or maintain consistent connectivity with shore-based resources. Extreme weather, fog, precipitation, and frigid temperatures can reduce the effectiveness of radar and optical sensors, making it more difficult to identify hazards above the surface. These challenges are amplified by the isolation of polar operations. Search and rescue efforts in these regions face extreme logistical difficulties, complicating both the detection of vessels in distress and the ability to safely reach them. An incident that might be relatively manageable in more populated waters can quickly become a serious emergency when support is far beyond reach. Groundings and collisions also present an increased risk to the surrounding environment. Oil spills and other pollution incidents are particularly difficult to contain in polar waters due to harsh operating conditions, limited infrastructure, and restricted response capabilities. These regions are also home to numerous native and migratory whale species, many of which are endangered. Vessel strikes remain a significant human-caused threat to whales, further elevating the environmental consequences of maritime operations. Underwater Perception Solution For 25 years, FarSounder has developed Argos 3D Forward Looking Sonar systems designed to provide real-time situational awareness of what lies beneath the surface ahead of the vessel. Argos sonars provide a real-time 3D image of the water column and seafloor out to distances of up to 1000 meters, enabling operators to make informed decisions before hazards become immediate threats. The Argos system’s low-frequency operation ensures that acoustic output remains benign to marine life, while still enabling the detection of large marine mammals such as whales. Ice, in particular, is an ideal sonar target. Its dense, reflective structure produces strong acoustic returns, allowing Argos systems to detect submerged ice masses that lie beneath the surface. At the same time, it maps the seafloor ahead at ranges of at least eight times the water depth below the sensor. In poorly charted or uncharted waters, this capability reveals shallows and obstructions like rocky pinnacles extending from the seafloor and moving hazards in the water column, including whales. In environments where GPS is degraded, communications are intermittent, and charts are unreliable, Argos systems continue to deliver consistent, real-time data. With a rapid update rate and the ability to scan from the seafloor to the surface in a single ping, operators gain a continuous understanding of the space ahead Polar Charts: Unreliable, Outdated, or Non-Existent Beyond underwater perception ahead, Argos sonars also create a map of the collected seafloor data. These recorded depth measurements are recalled when returning to a previous location, allowing vessels to identify and follow safe routes where chart data is unreliable. The sonar’s software enables this data to be anonymously shared across the FarSounder fleet . In return, vessels will gain access to an aggregate map of all other customer contributions. This program also supports global ocean mapping initiatives like Seabed 2030 . These crowdsourcing efforts have been able to provide tangible value for the broader maritime community operating in Arctic regions. FarSounder’s crowdsourced bathymetry (CSB) data is unique compared to most other CSB contributions in that it has high quality meta-data. This makes FarSounder customer CSB valuable in that it can be more reliably used for other applications. For example, because of the meta-data quality, CSB contributed by one of our customers transiting the Northwest Passage was included in an official chart produced by the Canadian Hydrographic Service. While poorly charted waters are an obvious concern for polar operators, the reliability of nautical charts is not exclusively an issue in remote regions. Even areas generally considered to be among the best surveyed and charted in the world can contain significant discrepancies between charted depths and actual seafloor conditions. Work conducted by Anthony Klemm, Physical Scientist at NOAA’s Coast Survey Development Lab, comparing crowdsourced bathymetry and satellite-derived bathymetry (SDB) with NOAA’s BlueTopo database and official nautical charts, has identified numerous locations where charted depths differ dramatically from measured conditions. One example involved a FarSounder customer transiting off the coast of Massachusetts near Nantucket. During the voyage, the vessel passed over a shoal charted to be approximately 10–12 meters deep. However, measurements collected by the vessel’s Argos sonar indicated that the actual depth was closer to 5 meters. The measured data was shared through the IHO Data Centre for Digital Bathymetry (DCDB). Anthony analyzed the contribution and found that the shoal identified in the crowdsourced data correlated with a seafloor trend visible in satellite-derived bathymetry for the same location. Fortunately, the transiting vessel was a relatively shallow-draft pleasure craft. However, had a larger commercial vessel passed over the same shoal, particularly at low tide, the discrepancy could have resulted in a grounding. This example is not an isolated occurrence. Using crowdsourced bathymetry data, Anthony has been developing automated tools to identify additional locations where charted depths may not accurately reflect actual conditions, including waters generally considered to be among the best charted areas in the world. These findings highlight an important consideration for maritime operators: even official nautical charts cannot always be relied upon to provide a complete representation of the underwater environment. In remote polar regions, where hydrographic survey coverage is significantly limited, the potential for encountering unknown hazards is even greater. Improving Awareness in the World’s Most Remote Waters For FarSounder, these challenges are not simply theoretical. Argos 3D Forward Looking Sonars have been installed on ice-classed hulls, icebreakers, and customer vessels that regularly operate in polar regions for more than two decades. Expedition cruise ships and explorer yachts leverage this technology to reach remote destinations, providing truly unique experiences for guests onboard. Icebreakers, naval ships, and research vessels are able to identify submerged ice and underwater obstacles, helping to reduce risk and extend operations into locations critical to their missions. Customers have experienced firsthand the difference that real-time underwater awareness can make in these environments. Ice Pilot Captain Clive Shute described his first experience using Argos while navigating ice-rich waters off Greenland: “I was lucky to have the opportunity to use FarSounder’s Argos Forward Looking Sonar for the first time recently. We were taking the ship in the ice-rich waters off Greenland. Having the Argos system installed proved to be a game-changer in safety.” Other customers have shared examples of Argos identifying hazards that conventional navigation tools failed to reveal. Captain Walter Wetmore described an instance where the system identified a shoreline that was incorrectly represented on the chart, helping the vessel avoid a potential grounding and avoid floating ice while navigating fjords: “The system clearly showed a shoreline, which was incorrectly shown on the chart, and helped avoid a grounding. It also showed growlers and bergy bits when traveling up the fjords. I will not travel to areas of ice again without the FarSounder systems.” For some operators, the technology has become an essential part of their ability to undertake these voyages in the first place. Reflecting on the capabilities Argos sonars provides while exploring remote polar waters, the owner of MY Warbird offered a simple but powerful statement: “We would not have gone that far north without the FarSounder.” As more sectors of the maritime industry shift their focus toward polar regions, the need for reliable, real-time underwater perception will continue to grow. FarSounder’s technology provides an innovative solution backed by 25 years of experience supporting those operating in some of the world’s most challenging maritime environments. articles.title: Container freight rates remain under pressure as major benchmarks decline
articles.summary: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly assessments, with Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) and three major Chinese freight benchmarks declining, while the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recorded a modest increase. Drewry’s WCI fell 2% to US$4,305 per 40-foot container in its 12...
articles.body: Global container freight rates remained under pressure in the latest weekly assessments, with Drewry’s World Container Index (WCI) and three major Chinese freight benchmarks declining, while the Freightos Baltic Index (FBX) recorded a modest increase. Drewry’s WCI fell 2% to US$4,305 per 40-foot container in its 12 November assessment, extending its recent downward movement. Meanwhile, the FBX Global Container Freight Index increased 1% to US$3,485. The Shanghai Containerized Freight Index (SCFI), China Containerized Freight Index (CCFI) and Ningbo Containerized Freight Index (NCFI) all declined in their 13 November readings. The NYSHEX Freight Index (NYFI) presented a more varied picture, with increases on Asia-US West Coast, Asia-North Europe and Transatlantic Westbound, contrasting with declines on Asia-US East Coast and Transatlantic Eastbound. Chinese freight indexes decline The SCFI decreased 1.68% to 3,572.33 points on 13 November, compared with 3,633.45 in the previous assessment. The CCFI declined approximately 0.28% to 1,919.27 points from 1,924.69 a week earlier, reversing the increase recorded in the preceding reading. The NCFI fell approximately 1.18% to 2,414.46 points, compared with 2,443.24 previously. All three Chinese composite benchmarks therefore moved lower, although the extent of the declines varied. The SCFI recorded the largest percentage decrease, followed by the NCFI, while the CCFI showed a relatively limited adjustment. NYFI shows contrasting Transpacific movements The NYFI assessment published on 13 November revealed different developments across the two major Transpacific routes. Asia-US West Coast increased 0.64% to 7,874.07, compared with 7,823.86 a week earlier, extending the route’s recent upward movement. Asia-US East Coast, however, declined 3.71% to 9,727.11 from 10,101.42 in the previous assessment. The contrast was notable because the West Coast continued to record modest gains while the East Coast experienced a more substantial weekly decrease. On Asia-North Europe, the NYFI increased 1.84% to 3,228.59 from 3,170.40, reversing the previous week’s 1.04% decline. The increase suggests a firmer latest reading for the route, although its recent weekly movements have alternated between gains and losses. Transatlantic rates move in opposite directions The NYFI also recorded diverging movements across the Transatlantic market. Westbound rates increased 1.76% to 2,890.15 from 2,840.25, recovering part of the decrease recorded in the preceding assessment. Eastbound rates continued to decline, falling 3.83% to 1,017.84 from 1,058.39. The latest Eastbound decrease followed a 5.86% decline in the previous week, extending the downward movement on the route. Overall, three of the five NYFI trade lanes recorded increases, while two declined. The movements underline the importance of examining individual routes rather than relying exclusively on composite benchmarks. Drewry WCI extends downward movement Drewry’s WCI declined 2% to US$4,305 per 40-foot container on 12 November, compared with US$4,389 in the previous assessment. The decrease reflected weaker freight rates on both the Transpacific and Asia-Europe trade lanes. Shanghai-Los Angeles fell 2% to US$7,416 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-New York declined 3% to US$9,020. On Asia-Europe, Shanghai-Rotterdam decreased 3% to US$3,504 per 40-foot container, while Shanghai-Genoa remained stable at US$4,168. According to Drewry’s latest assessment , carriers are continuing to adjust available capacity through blank sailings. On the Transpacific, eight blank sailings were announced for the following week, compared with four in the current week. Drewry expects further downward pressure on freight rates amid weak demand. On Asia-Europe, eight blank sailings were announced for the following week, compared with five in the current week. Carriers have also announced higher Freight All Kinds (FAK) rates and Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) for the second half of November. Drewry expects these capacity adjustments and announced increases to provide some support to Asia-Europe rates in the coming weeks, although the actual outcome remains uncertain. FBX Global Index edges higher The FBX Global Container Freight Index increased approximately 1% to US$3,485, compared with US$3,452 in the preceding assessment. The increase followed two consecutive weekly declines, indicating a modest recovery in the global benchmark. However, the movement contrasted with the continued decline in Drewry’s WCI and the negative readings recorded by all three Chinese composite indexes. The difference reinforces the need to consider the methodologies and market coverage of each benchmark when assessing overall freight rate developments. Asia-Europe and Transpacific assessments diverge The latest figures reveal particularly interesting differences between the NYFI and Drewry assessments. On Asia-North Europe, NYFI increased 1.84%, while Drewry’s Shanghai-Rotterdam route declined 3%. Similarly, NYFI Asia-US West Coast rose 0.64%, contrasting with the 2% decrease recorded by Drewry on Shanghai-Los Angeles. On the US East Coast, however, both benchmarks indicated weaker conditions. NYFI Asia-US East Coast declined 3.71%, while Drewry Shanghai-New York fell 3%. These differences should not be interpreted as direct contradictions. NYFI is based on reported transactions involving containers that have actually shipped, while Drewry’s WCI assesses spot freight rates across selected routes. Their methodologies, route definitions and reporting periods differ, meaning the two indexes can reflect different short-term developments within related markets. Market outlook The latest assessments indicate continued weakness across several major container freight benchmarks, although individual trade lanes are not moving uniformly. The WCI recorded another weekly decline, while SCFI, CCFI and NCFI also moved lower. In contrast, the FBX recovered slightly and three NYFI routes posted increases. Drewry expects continued pressure on Transpacific freight rates amid weak demand, despite carriers’ efforts to manage capacity through blank sailings. On Asia-Europe, the impact of announced FAK increases, additional surcharges and capacity adjustments will be important to monitor in subsequent assessments. For now, the latest figures point to an uneven container freight market, with broader benchmark weakness accompanied by selective improvements on individual trade lanes.

articles.summary: The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity...
