Photo courtesy DP World The United Kingdom has launched a consultation on new maritime fuel regulations that could require thousands of ships calling at British ports to progressively reduce the greenhouse gas emissions intensity of their fuels beginning in 2030. The Department for Transport’s proposal , published Monday, November 16, would establish a fuel standard broadly aligned with the European Union’s FuelEU Maritime regulation while leaving room for adjustments as international negotiations at the International Maritime Organization (IMO) continue. Under the government’s preferred approach, the rules would initially apply to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above, regardless of flag, covering approximately 5,000 vessels based on historical port-call data. The proposed framework would regulate all energy used on domestic voyages between UK ports, 50% of energy used on international voyages to and from the UK, and energy consumed by covered ships while at berth in British ports. Rather than mandating particular fuels, the regulation would establish progressively tightening limits on the lifecycle greenhouse gas emissions intensity of energy consumed by ships. Operators could meet those requirements through alternative fuels, electrification and other lower-emission energy sources. The government is also considering compliance flexibility mechanisms, including pooling, banking and borrowing emissions credits, similar to provisions under FuelEU Maritime. However, several important details remain undecided, including how quickly emissions limits would tighten and whether the UK should follow the EU’s trajectory, align with future IMO standards or establish its own targets. The government expects the regulation to take effect from 2030. The UK Chamber of Shipping welcomed the consultation but urged policymakers to ensure that new requirements reflect the availability of alternative fuels, supporting infrastructure and commercially viable technologies. “We welcome the Government moving forward with this consultation. Greater long-term certainty can help unlock the investment needed to decarbonise shipping, but regulation needs to develop alongside the fuels, infrastructure and technology that operators will need,” a Chamber spokesperson said. “Any future UK framework must be practical, support investment and maintain the international competitiveness of UK shipping.” The Chamber has previously called for a regulatory framework that avoids duplicating existing international requirements while providing operators with sufficient flexibility to manage the transition. In an October policy paper, the organization recommended aligning fuel certification and lifecycle emissions accounting with emerging IMO standards, developing reliable monitoring and verification systems, and setting targets based on realistic assessments of fuel availability and infrastructure readiness. Those concerns are particularly relevant given the significant overlap between ships trading to the UK and those already subject to European regulations. According to the government’s consultation, approximately 97% of ships above 5,000 gross tonnage that called at UK ports in 2019 also called at EU ports. The consultation comes as the international shipping industry continues to grapple with uncertainty surrounding the IMO’s proposed global Net-Zero Framework. While the UK government acknowledges that international regulation remains the most effective way to reduce shipping emissions, it argues that uncertainty over global measures should not prevent domestic action. The proposed fuel regulation would complement the UK’s existing maritime carbon-pricing measures, including the extension of the UK Emissions Trading Scheme to domestic shipping in July 2026. The government is also seeking industry feedback on whether smaller ships should eventually be included, with vessels between 400 and 5,000 gross tonnage remaining under review. Beyond the emissions requirements themselves, the consultation examines the availability of alternative maritime fuels, bunkering infrastructure, port readiness and the investment needed to support widespread adoption. The Department for Transport has emphasized that its proposals are preliminary and that no final regulatory decisions have been made. The consultation remains open until February 22, 2027 . The UK Chamber of Shipping said it will work with its members and the UK Alternative Maritime Fuels Coalition to develop a detailed response addressing the operational, commercial and technical implications of the proposed framework. articles.title: Supertanker Rates Plunge More Than 60% From Record Highs
articles.summary: The cost of shipping oil in the largest tankers has declined sharply since the beginning of November, reflecting weaker demand for chartering and an unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium that sent shipping costs to a record high in October.
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Join the leading maritime news network Photo: Shutterstock/Sven Hansche LONDON, Nov 16 (Reuters) – The cost of shipping oil in the largest tankers has declined sharply since the beginning of November, reflecting weaker demand for chartering and an unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium that sent shipping costs to a record high in October. Freight ?rates for supertankers, also known as very large crude carriers (VLCCs), carrying ?oil from the Gulf of Oman to China fell to about 308 ?on the Worldscale basis on November 13, down by 64% from their record high of 841 on October 8, Baltic Exchange data shows. The plunge in rates came as Gulf oil exporters increased crude flows towards levels seen before the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran. The increase in flows has been achieved using workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers and so-called dark crossings, where tankers switch off tracking signals to evade detection, even as attacks against ships continued. The rise in Gulf oil exports reduced demand for crude shipped from other regions, freeing up VLCCs. “Gulf oil exports recently recovered to near prewar volumes, reducing Asian buyer demand for US and North Sea crudes, which in turn weighed on demand for tankers,” said Arrow Shipbroking analyst Delia He. Vortexa analyst Ioannis Papadimitriou said the recent spike in freight rates had reduced Asian demand for longer-haul US, West African and North Sea crude, which in turn increased the region’s use of Middle East crude, and that VLCC demand for longer voyages dropped as a result. “At the same time, vessel availability is building as ships discharge in East Asia,” he said. “As more tonnage is freed up, rates come under downward pressure.” EASING GEOPOLITICAL RISK PREMIUM Rates fell even more sharply on other routes, such as from West Africa to Asia. The jump in freight costs had been partly driven by factors including the perception of a higher risk of operating in the Middle East Gulf as Iran and the US attacked tankers, which had also pushed up oil prices. Oil prices LCOc1 have dropped by 20% this month, partly on the potential for de-escalation in the Iran war. “The sharp decline in freight rates is only partly driven by market fundamentals, as such a steep move reflects an exaggerated unwinding of the geopolitical risk premium,” Arrow’s He said. articles.title: ExxonMobil brings online its fifth oil project offshore Guyana
articles.summary: The start-up of production at Uaru raises Guyana’s installed capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 16, 2026 · 6 minutes ago ExxonMobil brings online its fifth oil project offshore Guyana The start-up of production at Uaru raises Guyana’s installed capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email FPSO Errea Wittu Source: MODEC ExxonMobil Guyana, a subsidiary of the U.S.-headquartered energy giant ExxonMobil, has put into production mode its fifth development in the Stabroek block off the coast of Guyana. A floating production, storage, and offloading (FPSO) vessel, which was constructed for deployment on this project, marks MODEC’s entry into Guyana's market, building on the company’s extensive experience in Brazil. ExxonMobil Guyana has confirmed the first oil from Uaru , its fifth development in the Stabroek block, lifting the country’s installed production capacity to 1.1 million barrels per day, as the FPSO Errea Wittu joins the Destiny , Unity , Prosperity , and One Guyana units. " The startup of Errea Wittu is another major milestone for Guyana and ExxonMobil. In just over a decade, Guyana has become one of the world’s fastest-growing and most important new sources of energy supply. Reaching 1.1 million barrels per day of installed capacity reflects the strength of this world-class resource, the success of our collaboration with the government and our co-venturers, and the contributions of thousands of Guyanese helping to build the country’s energy future. " — Dan Ammann ExxonMobil’s Upstream Company President Related Articles Fossil Energy MODEC’s FPSO reaches Guyana as ExxonMobil’s fifth oil project nears start-up 4 min read The Uaru field is estimated to hold more than 800 million barrels of oil. The FPSO Errea Wittu, deployed approximately 200 kilometers offshore Guyana at a water depth of 1,690 meters using a SOFEC spread mooring system, will be able to store around 2 million barrels of crude oil. This FPSO , said to mean “abundance” in the Warrau language, is expected to achieve its initial production capacity of 250,000 barrels per day in the first quarter of 2027. The operator emphasizes that Uaru marks another significant step in the development of the Stabroek block, which the company describes as one of the world’s most prolific offshore discoveries. ExxonMobil Guyana operates the Stabroek block and has a 45% interest, with Hess Guyana Exploration, part of Chevron, owning 30%, and CNOOC Petroleum Guyana holding the remaining 25%. Since 2015, the firm and its Stabroek block co-venturers have spent more than $3.9 billion with Guyanese vendors, supporting local businesses, workforce development, and economic growth. ExxonMobil recently made a final investment decision (FID) on Longtail , its eighth development on the Stabroek block. articles.summary: Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd are bringing three more Gemini Cooperation services back through the Red Sea and Suez Canal, marking another major step in the container shipping industry’s gradual return to...
articles.body: Advertise Forum Jobs Subscribe Grab a Seat at the Captain’s Table Essential news coupled with the finest maritime content sourced from across the globe. Suez Canal Authority/Handout via REUTERS Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd are bringing three more Gemini Cooperation services back through the Red Sea and Suez Canal, marking another major step in the container shipping industry’s gradual return to the shorter route between Asia and Europe. The carriers announced Monday that their AE1, AE2 and AE3 services will shift from sailing around Africa’s Cape of Good Hope to transiting the Suez Canal, with the changes taking effect between December 2026 and January 2027. The announcement builds on a series of earlier routing changes as the partners progressively restore Suez transits across their shared network. According to Maersk’s November 16 advisory, the transitions will begin with the AE2 service on December 4, followed by AE3 on December 20 and AE1 on January 14, 2027. The AE2 service, connecting Asia, Europe and the Middle East, will begin its revised rotation with the Mary Maersk departing from Ningbo. The AE3 service will follow with the Alette Maersk from Shanghai, while the AE1 transition will begin with the Damietta Express, also from Shanghai. The decision follows a broader return to the Suez corridor that has gathered momentum in recent months. In September, the two carriers announced the rerouting of four additional Gemini services — AE5, AE11, AE12 and ME2 — joining two services already using the canal. Earlier this month, Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd also announced the return of their ME1 service connecting India and Europe, with the first revised sailings scheduled for November 4 and 13. The latest changes extend that shift to more of the carriers’ main Asia-Europe services, reducing reliance on the significantly longer route around southern Africa. For container lines and shippers, the Suez route offers shorter voyages, lower fuel consumption and faster transit times compared with Cape of Good Hope diversions. Returning services to the canal can also free up vessel capacity that has been tied up by longer voyages. Still, the carriers stressed that the return remains dependent on regional security conditions. Maersk and Hapag-Lloyd said they will continue closely monitoring developments in the Middle East, with any further changes to the Gemini network dependent on continued stability in the Red Sea. The announcement underscores the industry’s growing willingness to restore regular Suez Canal operations, while stopping short of suggesting that security risks in the region have disappeared. articles.title: ONE raises Emergency Fuel Surcharge across global trades
articles.summary: Ocean Network Express (ONE) will revise its Emergency Fuel Surcharge (EFS) across long-haul and short-sea trades from 15 December 2026. The updated surcharge will apply to dry and refrigerated cargo, with different levels for long-haul headhaul and backhaul shipments. Under the revised structure, dry containers...
articles.body: Ocean Network Express (ONE) will revise its Emergency Fuel Surcharge (EFS) across long-haul and short-sea trades from 15 December 2026. The updated surcharge will apply to dry and refrigerated cargo, with different levels for long-haul headhaul and backhaul shipments. Under the revised structure, dry containers moving on long-haul headhaul trades will be subject to an EFS of US$180 per TEU. The corresponding charge for reefer cargo will be US$230 per TEU. For long-haul backhaul movements, ONE will apply a surcharge of US$90 per TEU for dry containers and US$115 per TEU for reefers. The same US$90 and US$115 rates will apply to dry and reefer cargo, respectively, across all short-sea trades. Scope Direction Dry Reefer All long-haul trades Headhaul US$180/TEU US$230/TEU All long-haul trades Backhaul US$90/TEU US$115/TEU All short-sea trades All directions US$90/TEU US$115/TEU The revised charges will take effect on 15 December 2026 for both non-FMC and FMC-regulated trades. The FMC scope includes the United States, American Samoa, Puerto Rico, Guam, Saipan and Hawaii. The same implementation date will also apply to Canada. ONE said the changes remain subject to any required regulatory approvals and notice periods. The surcharge will remain in effect until further notice.

articles.title: Höegh Autoliners partners with BYD for battery-powered Aurora vessel
articles.summary: Höegh Autoliners has signed an agreement with BYD Energy Storage to install marine battery systems on its upcoming Aurora No. 12 car carrier. The project will combine battery storage, solar panels and a shaft generator with propulsion capable of using ammonia. The companies signed the strategic and technical...
articles.body: Höegh Autoliners has signed an agreement with BYD Energy Storage to install marine battery systems on its upcoming Aurora No. 12 car carrier. The project will combine battery storage, solar panels and a shaft generator with propulsion capable of using ammonia. The companies signed the strategic and technical cooperation agreement on 9 November 2026 during COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye. Aurora No. 12 is scheduled for delivery and the start of commercial operations in May 2028. According to Höegh Autoliners, the vessel will be the first deep-sea car carrier to combine these energy technologies in a single integrated system. The installation is expected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by approximately 1,000 tonnes of CO₂ equivalent annually. However, this remains a projected reduction rather than an achieved operational result. Battery integration to improve onboard energy efficiency The new system will combine BYD Energy Storage batteries with a shaft generator and solar panels. Together, these technologies are intended to improve energy management and reduce fuel consumption. The vessel will also be equipped with propulsion technology capable of operating on ammonia from delivery. Ammonia does not produce CO₂ during combustion. However, its overall environmental performance depends on how the fuel is produced and on the management of other emissions associated with its use. Green ammonia also remains more expensive than conventional marine fuels, creating an additional challenge for its wider adoption. “This shows that shipping can take the lead in the green transition. We are combining every green technology available on one vessel capable of running on ammonia from day one. Nobody has done that on a deep-sea car carrier before,” said Andreas Enger, CEO, Höegh Autoliners. The cooperation will also allow both companies to gain operational experience with integrated energy systems for large ocean-going vessels. According to Höegh Autoliners, the project forms part of its wider efforts to develop lower-emission deep-sea transportation. Aurora Class programme expands to 18 vessels Aurora No. 12 belongs to Höegh Autoliners’ Aurora Class, a new generation of pure car and truck carriers (PCTCs). Each vessel can transport up to 9,100 cars. The company states that the class can reduce carbon emissions by up to 58% compared with conventional PCTCs. The vessels carry DNV ammonia-ready and methanol-ready notations, supporting the company’s transition towards alternative marine fuels. China Merchants Heavy Industry (Jiangsu) is building the Aurora fleet, while Everllence supplies the main engines. Other project partners include Kongsberg Maritime, DNV and vessel designer Deltamarin. Following an order for six additional ships in August 2026, the Aurora programme now comprises 18 vessels. Further options and reserved construction slots could increase the programme to 26 vessels. The latest battery agreement adds another technology to the fleet renewal programme. Höegh Autoliners aims to use the combination of alternative fuels and energy-efficient systems to reduce emissions from long-distance vehicle transportation.

articles.summary: First gas has started flowing from a field in the North Sea, bringing what Adura describes as vital UK energy resources ashore in time for winter.
articles.body: Exploration & Production November 16, 2026 · 11 minutes ago UK operator turns production taps on as first gas flows from $2.8 billion North Sea field First gas has started flowing from a field in the North Sea, bringing what Adura describes as vital UK energy resources ashore in time for winter. MC Melisa Cavcic Senior Editor 2 minutes read LinkedIn X Email Jackdaw platform Source: Adura Adura, an incorporated joint venture between UK-headquartered Shell and Norway’s Equinor, has brought online one of the North Sea’s most controversial gas projects, which is expected to power British homes and businesses. The first production comes less than a month after the North Sea Transition Authority (NSTA) granted development and production consent for the Jackdaw field off the coast of northeast Scotland to Adura. This project represents £2.1 billion ($2.77 billion) of investment. The company has emphasized that Jackdaw gas will funnel through the existing Shearwater production hub and onwards to the St Fergus gas terminal in Aberdeenshire before being supplied to homes and businesses across Britain. When it reaches peak production in the coming months, the project is expected to produce enough gas to heat the equivalent of around 1.4 million UK homes, helping to reduce Britain’s reliance on imported energy, including liquefied natural gas (LNG), which carries a higher emissions footprint. " Jackdaw is now helping to power Britain. This is a proud moment for everyone at Adura, and a testament to the professionalism, expertise and dedication of our colleagues and the world-class UK supply chain who have worked tirelessly to make it possible. At a time of considerable uncertainty around the world, Jackdaw will provide secure energy from our own waters to heat British homes and power our economy, while reducing our reliance on imports with higher emissions. " — Claire Mueller Jackdaw Project Director at Adura The UK operator underlines that Jackdaw will continue to support skilled employment, supply chain businesses, and economic activity throughout its producing life, while generating tax revenues that could help fund public services and investment in net zero projects. According to Adura, the start of production represents the culmination of years of work by skilled people and businesses across the UK, drawing on decades of expertise in the North Sea. Located approximately 250 kilometers east of Aberdeen, this field is expected to be among the lowest-emission developments on the UK Continental Shelf (UKCS), while supporting jobs and bolstering Britain’s energy security. Related Articles Authorities & Government North Sea gas field cleared for take-off: UK greenlights Jackdaw after legal storms 4 min read Jackdaw is the first new project to be brought on stream since Shell and Equinor’s joint venture company was established in December 2025; thus, the operator believes the project demonstrates the continuing importance of the North Sea in meeting Britain’s energy needs. Adura’s next major project is the £8.7 billion ($11.49 billion) Rosebank development west of Shetland, which is currently awaiting a decision on its approval from the UK government. These two projects are expected to generate £1.4 billion ($1.85 billion) in tax revenues before the end of this Parliament, rising to £3.8 billion ($5.02 billion) by the end of the next. " Jackdaw also demonstrates what can be achieved when Britain makes pragmatic, evidence-led decisions about the energy it needs, while properly accounting for our climate responsibilities. It is a positive step towards restoring confidence in the North Sea and among the skilled people and businesses who have built this industry over decades. As a British company, headquartered in Aberdeen, Adura is proud to be producing the oil and gas our country will continue to need for decades, to some of the highest safety and emissions standards in the world.
